title: Advanced Excel
tagline: Lookups, conditional analysis, data cleaning, finance and dashboards, with a checked lab in every module
summary: Go from competent to confident. Write formulas that survive copying, look things up in tables, answer business questions with SUMIFS and rankings, clean messy data, use dates and text, build pivot-style summaries and charts, price loans and investments, and finish with a working regional dashboard. Every module has working spreadsheet labs that check your formulas and explain what is missing.

modules.title: Smarter formulas
modules.summary: Write formulas that survive being copied, make decisions with IFS and SWITCH, tame errors, and design a sheet so it is easy to check.
modules.outcome: You can build a calculation once and trust it everywhere: mixed references, readable decisions, handled errors and visible assumptions.
modules.intro: Basic Excel teaches you to write a formula. Advanced Excel is about writing formulas that are correct when copied, easy to read a year later, and hard to break. This module gives you the four habits behind every reliable spreadsheet: reference the right way, decide clearly, expect errors, and keep assumptions in plain sight.

topics.title: Mixed references: lock one direction
topics.html:
You already know that B2 is relative (it moves when copied) and $B$2 is absolute (it never moves). Real models often need something in between: lock the column but let the row move, or lock the row but let the column move. These are mixed references.

The four kinds of reference
WrittenColumnRowTypical use
B2movesmovesA formula copied in any direction
$B$2lockedlockedA single input such as a tax rate
$B2lockedmovesAlways read column B, whichever column the formula is in
B$2moveslockedAlways read row 2, whichever row the formula is in
Worked example

A price grid in one formula

Prices run down column A (5, 8, 12) and order sizes run across row 1 (10, 20, 50). Every cell in the grid should be price times size.

  1. In B2 write =$A2*B$1.
  2. $A2: the column is locked, so the price always comes from column A; the row is free, so it follows the formula down.
  3. B$1: the row is locked, so the size always comes from row 1; the column is free, so it follows the formula across.
  4. Copy B2 across to D2 and down to row 4. Every cell finds its own price and its own size.

Answer. One formula fills nine cells correctly. The mistake to avoid is typing nine different formulas by hand.

Tip

Press F4 repeatedly while the cursor is in a reference. It cycles through B2, $B$2, B$2 and $B2, so you never need to type a dollar sign.

Watch out

A formula that looks right in the first cell can be wrong everywhere else. Always check the last cell of a copied block as well as the first.

Try it yourself: What does =$A2*B$1 become when copied from B2 to D4?

Model answer. In D4 it becomes =$A4*D$1. The column of the first reference stays A and the row of the second stays 1; the other parts moved.

Check what you just learned

1. Which reference always reads from row 1 but lets the column move?
  • $A1
  • A1
  • $A$1
  • A$1 (correct)

The dollar sign sits before the row number, so the row is locked and the column is free.

2. =$A2*B$1 is copied from B2 to C3. What does it become?
  • =$A3*C$1 (correct)
  • =$A2*C$1
  • =$A3*B$1
  • =$B3*C$1

Copying one column right moves B to C in the unlocked column part; copying one row down moves 2 to 3 in the unlocked row part.
keyPoints: A dollar sign locks whatever comes right after it.
$A2 locks the column; A$2 locks the row; $A$2 locks both.
Check the last cell of a copied block, not just the first.

topics.title: Logic that reads well: IF, AND, OR, IFS and SWITCH
topics.html:
A decision in a spreadsheet is a test and two or more answers. The classic tool is IF(test, if_true, if_false). When there are several bands, people nest one IF inside another, and the formula quickly becomes a maze of brackets. Two newer functions fix that.

Choosing the right decision function
You have...UseExample
One yes/no testIF=IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail")
Two or more conditions that must all be true or any be trueIF with AND / OR=IF(AND(B2>=40,C2>=40),"Pass","Fail")
Several bands, checked in orderIFS=IFS(B2>=90,"A",B2>=75,"B",TRUE,"C")
One value compared with exact matchesSWITCH=SWITCH(A2,1,"Low",2,"Medium",3,"High","Unknown")
Worked example

Commission bands with IFS

Sales of 100,000 or more earn 10%, from 60,000 earn 7%, from 30,000 earn 5%, anything lower earns 2%.

  1. Write =IFS(B2>=100000,0.1,B2>=60000,0.07,B2>=30000,0.05,TRUE,0.02).
  2. IFS checks each test from left to right and returns the answer beside the first true test.
  3. That is why the biggest band goes first: 120,000 passes the first test and stops there.
  4. The final TRUE,0.02 is a catch-all, like otherwise: it is always true, so anything that missed the other bands gets 2%.

Answer. A sale of 75,000 fails the 100,000 test, passes the 60,000 test, and earns 7%.

Try the bands

Move the sales figure and see which band applies.

Adjust Sales (rupees) and see Commission rate, Commission change.

When to prefer which

  • Nested IF only for two bands. Three or more levels is the signal to switch.
  • IFS for ranges and conditions, tested in order.
  • SWITCH for exact matches such as codes or numbers.
  • A lookup table (next module) when the bands change often: change the table, not every formula.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the smallest band first in IFS. The first true test wins, so a small threshold swallows everything above it.
  • Forgetting the catch-all TRUE. Without it IFS returns #N/A when nothing matches.
  • Using = comparisons on decimals that come from calculations; round first with ROUND.

Check what you just learned

1. In =IFS(B2>=90,"A",B2>=75,"B",TRUE,"C"), what does 80 give?
  • A
  • B (correct)
  • C
  • #N/A

80 fails the first test and passes the second.

2. Why end an IFS with TRUE?
  • To make it faster
  • To turn on checking
  • To catch everything that matched no other test (correct)
  • Excel requires it

TRUE is always true, so it works as the 'otherwise' answer.
keyPoints: IFS returns the answer for the first true test, so order matters.
End IFS with TRUE and a fallback so it never returns #N/A.
Use SWITCH for exact matches; use a lookup table when the bands change.

topics.title: Errors: expect them, explain them, handle them
topics.html:
An error is not a failure; it is Excel saying this cannot be worked out. Advanced users do two things with errors: read them to find the cause, and handle the ones that are expected.

What each error is telling you
ErrorMeaningFirst thing to check
#DIV/0!Dividing by zero or an empty cellThe cell you divide by
#VALUE!Maths on text, or the wrong kind of valueNumbers stored as text; a heading inside a range
#REF!A reference points at a cell that no longer existsDeleted rows or columns
#NAME?Excel does not know a nameSpelling of the function
#N/AA lookup found nothingWhether the key really exists, spelling and spaces
Worked example

Cost per unit with a zero

Cost is in B and units are in C. One item has zero units, so B/C would show #DIV/0! in the middle of a report.

  1. Wrap the division: =IFERROR(B3/C3,"n/a").
  2. IFERROR runs the first formula; only if it fails does it show the second value.
  3. Now a reader sees n/a for that row and real numbers for the others, and totals that skip text keep working.

Answer. Handle the error you expect; do not hide errors you do not understand.

IFERROR catches every kind of error, which can hide a real mistake such as a misspelled function. When you only expect a missing lookup, use IFNA, which catches #N/A and lets every other error show.

A safer way to handle errors

  • Find out why the error happens before wrapping it.
  • Use IFNA for lookups and IFERROR for divisions.
  • Show a clear message such as "missing", not a blank cell or a zero that looks real.
  • Keep one or two check cells that count errors, for example =SUMPRODUCT(--ISERROR(D2:D100)), so hidden problems are visible.
Watch out

Never use IFERROR to make a total look right. If a lookup fails and you replace it with 0, the report adds a wrong number with full confidence.

Try it yourself: A lookup returns #N/A for a product that is not on the price list. Should you hide it with IFERROR(...,0)?

Model answer. No. A price of 0 looks real and silently understates the order. Show a clear marker such as "not on price list" with IFNA, so someone fixes the list.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function catches only #N/A?
  • IFERROR
  • IFS
  • ISERROR
  • IFNA (correct)

IFNA is narrower, so other errors still show.

2. #DIV/0! most often means:
  • A divide by zero or an empty cell (correct)
  • A misspelled name
  • A deleted cell
  • A date problem

Check the cell you divide by.
keyPoints: Read the error first; handle only what you expect.
IFNA is safer than IFERROR for lookups.
A fake 0 is worse than a visible error.

topics.title: Build for the next person: assumptions and checks
topics.html:
Most spreadsheet disasters are not clever formulas gone wrong; they are numbers buried inside formulas that nobody remembers. A tax rate typed as *0.18 in forty cells cannot be changed safely. Professional models follow a few small rules.

Habits of a reliable model
HabitWhy it matters
Put every input in its own labelled cellChange it once and everything updates
Never type a number inside a formula that is really an assumptionHard-coded numbers hide and go stale
Keep inputs, calculations and results visibly separateReaders know where to look and what to change
Add a check cellA total that must equal another total will shout when it does not
Use one formula per row or column, copiedInconsistent formulas are the commonest source of errors
Worked example

Move the rate out of the formula

A sheet multiplies every price by 0.18 for tax. The rate changes next year.

  1. Put the rate in its own cell, say B1, with the label Tax rate.
  2. Rewrite each formula as =B4*$B$1.
  3. Add a check cell: the total of the tax column should equal the total price times the rate, for example =ROUND(SUM(C4:C20)-SUM(B4:B20)*B1,2) and it should show 0.

Answer. Now one change updates everything, and a nonzero check cell warns you when a formula was overwritten.

Tip

Use Formulas > Show Formulas (Ctrl and the backtick key) to look at the whole sheet as formulas. A formula that looks different from its neighbours is the one to inspect.

Common mistakes

  • Typing over a formula with a number 'just this once'. Mark the cell so everyone can see it is a manual override.
  • Mixing units (rupees and thousands) in one column.
  • Leaving test numbers in the file you send.

Check what you just learned

1. Where should a tax rate that changes yearly live?
  • Inside every formula
  • In its own labelled cell (correct)
  • In a comment
  • In the file name

A separate cell lets you change it once.

2. What does a check cell do?
  • Hides errors
  • Formats the sheet
  • Shows when two numbers that should agree do not (correct)
  • Locks the sheet

It makes a hidden mistake visible.

Key terms: flip and sort

Mixed reference
A reference with a $ on only the column or only the row
IFS
Tests conditions in order and returns the answer for the first true one
Catch-all
A final TRUE test that handles everything left over
IFERROR
Shows a fallback value if a formula returns any error
IFNA
Shows a fallback only when the error is #N/A
Check cell
A cell that compares two numbers which should agree
keyPoints: Inputs go in labelled cells, not inside formulas.
A check cell turns a silent mistake into a visible one.
One consistent formula per column is easier to trust.

modules.title: Lookups and matching
modules.summary: Find values in tables with VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, use approximate matches for bands, and avoid the traps that return wrong answers.
modules.outcome: You can pull the right price, rate, name or band from a table for any row, and explain why each lookup works.
modules.intro: Almost every business sheet has a table you look things up in: a price list, a tax slab, a staff directory, a grade scale. Typing those values by hand is slow and error-prone. Lookups let one small table feed hundreds of rows, and changing the table changes every answer.

topics.title: VLOOKUP: look down a table
topics.html:
VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table, column_number, match_type) finds a key in the first column of a table and returns the value from the column you name, in the same row.

The four parts of VLOOKUP
PartWhat to give itExample
lookup_valueThe key you are searching forA2 (a product code)
tableThe block of cells, with the key in its first column$G$2:$I$5
column_numberWhich column of the table to return (1 is the first)3 for the price
match_typeFALSE for an exact matchFALSE
Worked example

Price an order line

The price list is in G2:I5 (Code, Item, Price). Cell A2 holds the code P3.

  1. Item name: =VLOOKUP(A2,$G$2:$I$5,2,FALSE) returns Bag.
  2. Price: =VLOOKUP(A2,$G$2:$I$5,3,FALSE) returns 800.
  3. The table reference is locked with dollar signs so it stays put when you copy the formula down.
  4. Amount: =B2*D2 multiplies quantity by the looked-up price.

Answer. Change the price list once and every order line updates.

Watch out

VLOOKUP can only look right of the key column. If the key is in column C and the answer is in column A, VLOOKUP cannot do it. That is one reason XLOOKUP and INDEX with MATCH are preferred.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving out FALSE. Without it VLOOKUP assumes a sorted table and can return the wrong row quietly.
  • Forgetting to lock the table with $. The table slides down as you copy and rows start to return #N/A.
  • Counting the column number from the sheet instead of from the table: it is the position inside the table.
  • Keys with trailing spaces or numbers stored as text: the key looks identical but does not match.
Try it yourself: Your table is B2:E9 and you need the value in column D. What column number do you give?

Model answer. 3. Count inside the table: B is 1, C is 2, D is 3.

Check what you just learned

1. In VLOOKUP(A2,$G$2:$I$5,3,FALSE), what does 3 mean?
  • The third row
  • Round to 3 places
  • Three matches
  • The third column of the table (correct)

The column number counts inside the table.

2. Why add FALSE?
  • To find an exact match (correct)
  • To sort the table
  • To lock the table
  • To hide errors

FALSE asks for an exact match.
keyPoints: VLOOKUP searches the first column and returns from a column you name.
Always give FALSE for an exact match, and lock the table.
It cannot look to the left of the key column.

topics.title: Approximate match: finding the band
topics.html:
Sometimes you do not want an exact match; you want to know which band a number falls into: a discount slab, a tax bracket, a letter grade, a commission tier. For this, use an approximate match with TRUE (or leave the last value out).

A discount table, sorted from smallest to largest
Spend fromDiscount
00%
1,0005%
5,00010%
10,00015%

With TRUE, VLOOKUP looks for the largest start that is not above your value, and returns that band's answer. A spend of 2,500 returns 5% (the band starting at 1,000); a spend of exactly 5,000 returns 10%; 12,000 returns 15%.

Worked example

Discount slabs

The band table is in F2:G5, the spend is in B2.

  1. Discount: =VLOOKUP(B2,$F$2:$G$5,2,TRUE).
  2. Amount to pay: =B2*(1-C2).
  3. Spend 800 returns 0% because the first band starts at 0; spend 12,000 returns 15%.

Answer. Changing a band (say 5% from 1,500) means editing one cell, not every formula.

Watch out

The table must be sorted ascending by the first column, and it must start low enough to catch the smallest value. If the first band started at 1,000, a spend of 800 would give #N/A.

Where does the spend land?

Move the spend and watch the band and the amount to pay.

Adjust Spend (rupees) and see Discount, To pay change.

Check what you just learned

1. With bands starting at 0, 1000, 5000 and 10000, what band does 5000 fall in?
  • The 1000 band
  • The 5000 band (correct)
  • The 10000 band
  • #N/A

A value equal to a band start belongs to that band.

2. What breaks an approximate match?
  • A sorted table
  • A locked table
  • A table that is not sorted ascending (correct)
  • A number key

The method assumes ascending order.
keyPoints: TRUE finds the largest start not above the value.
The first column must be sorted ascending and start low enough.
Edit the table, not the formulas, when bands change.

topics.title: INDEX and MATCH: the flexible pair
topics.html:
MATCH(value, range, 0) tells you the position of a value in a list. INDEX(range, position) returns the item at a position. Together they find anything, in any direction, without counting columns.

What each one does
FunctionQuestion it answersExampleResult
MATCHWhere is it in the list?=MATCH("Bag",B2:B5,0)3
INDEXWhat is at this position?=INDEX(C2:C5,3)the third price
TogetherWhat is the price of the Bag?=INDEX(C2:C5,MATCH("Bag",B2:B5,0))800
Worked example

A two-way lookup

Quarterly sales are in B2:E5. Regions are in A2:A5 and quarters in B1:E1. You want South in Q3.

  1. Row: MATCH("South",A2:A5,0) gives 2.
  2. Column: MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0) gives 3.
  3. Combine them: =INDEX(B2:E5,MATCH("South",A2:A5,0),MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0)).
  4. INDEX goes to row 2, column 3 of B2:E5 and returns 110.

Answer. Put the region and quarter in input cells and the same formula answers any question.

Why many experts prefer INDEX and MATCH to VLOOKUP

  • It can return a value to the left of the key.
  • It does not break when someone inserts a column in the table.
  • It can look up across rows and down columns at once.
  • MATCH with 0 is always an exact match: there is no TRUE/FALSE to forget.
Tip

To find the name that goes with the biggest number: =INDEX(A2:A5,MATCH(MAX(E2:E5),E2:E5,0)). MAX finds the number, MATCH finds its position, INDEX returns the name.

Common mistakes

  • Using ranges of different shapes: the range inside MATCH must line up with the range inside INDEX.
  • Forgetting the 0 in MATCH. Without it MATCH guesses with an approximate match.
  • Hard-typing the row or column number instead of using MATCH, which breaks when the table is re-sorted.

Check what you just learned

1. What does =MATCH("Bag",B2:B5,0) return if Bag is the third item?
  • Bag
  • #N/A
  • 800
  • 3 (correct)

MATCH returns a position.

2. Which pair finds the name that goes with the largest value?
  • INDEX and MATCH with MAX (correct)
  • SUM and COUNT
  • IF and AND
  • LEFT and RIGHT

MAX finds the value, MATCH its position, INDEX the name.
keyPoints: MATCH returns a position; INDEX returns the item at a position.
Use two MATCHes inside INDEX for a two-way lookup.
Use MATCH(...,0) so it is always exact.

topics.title: XLOOKUP, and choosing the right lookup
topics.html:
XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_range, return_range, if_not_found) is the modern lookup. It searches one range and returns from another, so the answer can be in any column, and it has a built-in answer for "not found".

Worked example

Price by item name

Items are in B2:B5 and prices in C2:C5.

  1. =XLOOKUP("Book",B2:B5,C2:C5) returns 45.
  2. Add a fallback: =XLOOKUP("Lamp",B2:B5,C2:C5,"not on price list") shows the message instead of #N/A.
  3. The lookup range and the return range can be any two columns, in any order.

Answer. No column numbers to count, no TRUE or FALSE to remember.

Which lookup should you use?
SituationBest choice
You have a current Excel with XLOOKUP, and a simple key and answerXLOOKUP
You must support older Excel versions or Google Sheets style filesINDEX and MATCH (or VLOOKUP for a quick job)
The answer is to the left of the keyXLOOKUP or INDEX and MATCH
You want a band (a slab or grade)VLOOKUP with TRUE or MATCH with 1
You need a value at the crossing of a row and a columnINDEX with two MATCHes
Watch out

The Yugty practice sheet teaches the lookup ideas with VLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, which work in every version of Excel and in other spreadsheet tools. XLOOKUP is available in current Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 or later; check your version before relying on it in a shared file.

Three checks before you trust any lookup

  • Does the key really exist in the table (spelling, spaces, numbers stored as text)?
  • Is the lookup range exactly the same size as the return range?
  • Did you test one row by hand?
Try it yourself: A report must run in an office that still uses an old Excel. Which lookup is safest?

Model answer. INDEX with MATCH, or VLOOKUP. XLOOKUP is not in older versions.

Check what you just learned

1. Which lookup has a built-in answer for 'not found'?
  • VLOOKUP
  • XLOOKUP (correct)
  • MATCH
  • INDEX

XLOOKUP's fourth value is what to show when nothing matches.

2. A band (like a discount slab) is best found with:
  • COUNT
  • XLOOKUP with an exact match
  • VLOOKUP with TRUE (correct)
  • ROUND

An approximate match returns the band a number falls into.

Key terms: flip and sort

Lookup value
The key you search for
Table array
The block of cells a lookup searches
Exact match
Only a key that is identical counts
Approximate match
Finds the largest start not above the value, for bands
MATCH
Returns the position of a value in a list
INDEX
Returns the item at a position
keyPoints: XLOOKUP returns from any column and has a not-found answer.
INDEX with MATCH works everywhere and in any direction.
Test one row by hand before copying a lookup down.

modules.title: Conditional analysis
modules.summary: Answer business questions with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS, rank and extract the top items, and weigh results with SUMPRODUCT.
modules.outcome: You can turn a long table into precise answers: totals, counts and averages for any combination of conditions, plus rankings and shares.
modules.intro: Managers ask questions with conditions: What did the North sell in Pens? How many Book orders were over three units? Who are the top three? Conditional functions answer them from the raw data, so you never have to sort, filter and add by hand.

topics.title: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS
topics.html:
You met SUMIF and COUNTIF in the basics: one condition. The IFS family handles several conditions at once, and every condition must be true for a row to count.

The IFS family
FunctionAnswersPattern
SUMIFSTotal of ... where ...=SUMIFS(sum_range, range1, cond1, range2, cond2)
COUNTIFSHow many rows where ...=COUNTIFS(range1, cond1, range2, cond2)
AVERAGEIFSAverage of ... where ...=AVERAGEIFS(avg_range, range1, cond1)
MAXIFS / MINIFSLargest or smallest ... where ...=MAXIFS(max_range, range1, cond1)
Worked example

Five questions, five formulas

Orders are in A2:D9 (Region, Product, Units, Revenue).

  1. North revenue: =SUMIFS(D2:D9,A2:A9,"North").
  2. Pen units sold in the South: =SUMIFS(C2:C9,B2:B9,"Pen",A2:A9,"South").
  3. Book orders over 3 units: =COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"Book",C2:C9,">3").
  4. Average Pen revenue: =AVERAGEIFS(D2:D9,B2:B9,"Pen").
  5. Largest North order: =MAXIFS(D2:D9,A2:A9,"North").

Answer. Each answer is one formula pointing at the raw data, so it updates when the data changes.

Writing conditions
You wantWriteExample
Equal to text"North"A2:A9,"North"
Equal to a cellthe cellA2:A9,F2
Greater than a number">3"C2:C9,">3"
At least a cell's value">="&F2C2:C9,">="&F2
Not equal"<>Book"B2:B9,"<>Book"

Common mistakes

  • Ranges of different sizes in one formula give #VALUE!.
  • Putting the sum range last in SUMIFS: it comes first (unlike SUMIF).
  • Typing a comparison without quotes, such as >3 instead of ">3".
  • Counting numbers stored as text: the condition silently fails to match.
Try it yourself: Write a formula for the total revenue of Book orders in the East.

Model answer. =SUMIFS(D2:D9,B2:B9,"Book",A2:A9,"East"). The sum range goes first, then a pair for each condition.

Check what you just learned

1. In SUMIFS, which argument comes first?
  • The first condition
  • A sheet name
  • The criteria cell
  • The range to add (correct)

SUMIFS starts with the range whose numbers are added.

2. What does COUNTIFS(B2:B9,"Book",C2:C9,">3") count?
  • Rows that are Book and over 3 units (correct)
  • Book rows or rows over 3
  • All rows
  • Only text

Every condition has to be true for the same row.
keyPoints: Every condition in an IFS formula must be true for a row to count.
In SUMIFS the range to add comes first; in COUNTIFS there is none.
Put comparisons in quotes, and join a cell with &.

topics.title: Ranking and the top N
topics.html:
Rankings answer who is first? and who are the top three? Three functions do the work, and INDEX with MATCH turns the answers into names.

Ranking tools
FunctionWhat it doesExample
RANKThe position of a value in a list (1 is highest)=RANK(B2,$B$2:$B$8)
LARGEThe k-th biggest value=LARGE($B$2:$B$8,2)
SMALLThe k-th smallest value=SMALL($B$2:$B$8,1)
Worked example

The top three students

Scores are in B2:B8.

  1. Rank for each student: =RANK(B2,$B$2:$B$8), with the range locked.
  2. The three highest scores: =LARGE($B$2:$B$8,1), then 2, then 3.
  3. The name for the first score: =INDEX($A$2:$A$8,MATCH(E2,$B$2:$B$8,0)).
  4. Copy down to get all three names.

Answer. A live leaderboard that updates when a score changes.

Watch out

If two people tie, RANK gives them the same rank and MATCH finds only the first match for the score. For a leaderboard where ties are possible, add a tiny tie-breaker (for example the row number divided by a million) to the scores in a helper column.

Tip

Lock the range inside RANK ($B$2:$B$8). If it slides down, each row ranks against a different, shrinking list.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function gives the second biggest value?
  • RANK
  • LARGE with k=2 (correct)
  • SMALL with k=2
  • MAX

LARGE(range,2) is the second largest.

2. Why lock the range in RANK?
  • To colour it
  • To sort it
  • So every row ranks against the whole list (correct)
  • To hide it

Otherwise the range slides as you copy the formula down.
keyPoints: RANK shows a position; LARGE and SMALL show values.
INDEX with MATCH turns a top value into a name.
Lock the ranked range; ties need a tie-breaker.

topics.title: Weights, shares and SUMPRODUCT
topics.html:
SUMPRODUCT(range1, range2) multiplies matching cells and adds the results: perfect for weighted averages, totals of price times quantity, and conditional sums over several ranges.

Worked example

A weighted grade

Maths counts 40%, Science 30% and English 30%. The scores are 80, 70 and 90.

  1. Weights in B2:B4, scores in C2:C4.
  2. =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B4,C2:C4) calculates 0.4*80 + 0.3*70 + 0.3*90.
  3. The result is 32 + 21 + 27 = 80.

Answer. A simple average (80) happens to match here; change one weight and they differ.

Formula · Share of a total

share = value / SUM($B$9:$B$11)

Lock the total with dollar signs so every row divides by the same number. Format the result as a percentage.

Units sold and each product's share
ProductUnitsShare
Pen4040%
Book3535%
Bag2525%

Change the weights

Move the weights and see the weighted grade change.

Adjust Maths weight (%), Science weight (%) and see English weight (what is left), Weighted grade (scores 80, 70, 90) change.

Common mistakes

  • Weights that do not add to 100%: always check with SUM.
  • Ranges of different sizes in SUMPRODUCT.
  • A share formula with an unlocked total, which gives a different denominator in every row.

Check what you just learned

1. What does SUMPRODUCT(B2:B4,C2:C4) do?
  • Adds B and C
  • Averages B
  • Counts cells
  • Multiplies matching cells and adds the products (correct)

It pairs the cells up, multiplies each pair and adds.

2. Weights of 40%, 30% and 20% add to:
  • 90% (correct)
  • 100%
  • 110%
  • 70%

They should add to 100%, so something is missing.

Key terms: flip and sort

SUMIFS
Adds numbers in rows where every condition is true
COUNTIFS
Counts rows where every condition is true
Criteria
The condition a row must meet, such as ">3"
RANK
Position of a value in a list
LARGE
The k-th largest value
SUMPRODUCT
Multiplies matching cells and adds the results
keyPoints: SUMPRODUCT multiplies matching cells and adds them.
Weights should add to 100%.
A share divides by a locked total and is formatted as a percentage.

modules.title: Text, dates and data cleaning
modules.summary: Clean messy text, split and join values, do arithmetic with dates, and format results for people to read.
modules.outcome: You can take a messy export, make it consistent, and build the labels, dates and deadlines a report needs.
modules.intro: Real data is rarely tidy. Names arrive in capitals, codes hide three facts in one cell, dates are typed ten ways, and numbers turn into text. Analysts say they spend most of their time cleaning. The functions in this module turn that into a few formulas.

topics.title: Cleaning text: TRIM, PROPER, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTITUTE
topics.html:
Data typed by people is full of small inconsistencies: extra spaces, MIXED capitals, odd punctuation. These break lookups (a trailing space makes "Asha" and "Asha " different keys) and make reports look careless.

The cleaning kit
FunctionFixesExampleResult
TRIMExtra spaces at the ends and between words=TRIM(" asha rao ")asha rao
PROPERCapitalises each word=PROPER("asha rao")Asha Rao
UPPER / LOWERAll capitals or all lowercase=LOWER("ASHA")asha
SUBSTITUTEReplaces one piece of text with another=SUBSTITUTE("98-765-43210","-","")9876543210
LENCounts characters (find hidden spaces)=LEN(A2)a number
Worked example

Clean a name list

Names such as asha RAO and chitra nair need to be tidy.

  1. Chain two functions: =PROPER(TRIM(A2)).
  2. TRIM runs first and removes the extra spaces; PROPER then fixes the capitals.
  3. Result: Asha Rao and Chitra Nair.

Answer. Nested functions run from the inside out.

Tip

To check whether two cells that look the same really match, compare their lengths: =LEN(A2)=LEN(B2). A hidden space shows up at once.

Watch out

Formulas leave the original data untouched, in another column. Keep the raw column: you may need to re-run the cleaning when new data arrives.

Common mistakes

  • Cleaning with find and replace and losing the original data.
  • Forgetting that PROPER also changes things like "McDonald" to "Mcdonald": check names that matter.
  • Using TRIM on a number stored as text and expecting it to become a number: use VALUE for that.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function removes the extra spaces between words?
  • PROPER
  • TRIM (correct)
  • LEN
  • LEFT

TRIM removes extra spaces at the ends and between words.

2. =PROPER(TRIM(" bilal KHAN ")) gives:
  • bilal khan
  • BILAL KHAN
  • Bilal Khan (correct)
  • Bilal Khan

TRIM tidies the spaces and PROPER fixes the capitals.
keyPoints: TRIM, PROPER, UPPER and LOWER make text consistent.
SUBSTITUTE swaps one piece of text for another.
Clean in a new column and keep the raw data.

topics.title: Splitting and joining: LEFT, MID, RIGHT, FIND, &, TEXT
topics.html:
Codes often pack several facts into one cell: IN-2026-0042 is a country, a year and a serial number. Text functions pull the pieces apart; the & operator and TEXT put them back together.

Cutting text
FunctionWhat it takesExample on IN-2026-0042Result
LEFT(text, n)n characters from the start=LEFT(A2,2)IN
MID(text, start, n)n characters from a position=MID(A2,4,4)2026
RIGHT(text, n)n characters from the end=RIGHT(A2,4)0042
FIND(text, within)The position of a character=FIND("-",A2)3
Worked example

Split, convert, rebuild

From IN-2026-0042 you need the year as a number and a label INV-0042.

  1. Year: =VALUE(MID(A2,4,4)) gives the number 2026. VALUE turns text into a number you can calculate with.
  2. Serial: =VALUE(RIGHT(A2,4)) gives 42.
  3. Label: ="INV-"&TEXT(D2,"0000") pads the number to four digits: INV-0042.

Answer. Cut with LEFT, MID, RIGHT; convert with VALUE; rebuild with & and TEXT.

Useful TEXT formats
FormatResult forShows
0000420042
#,##0.001234.51,234.50
0.0%0.25625.6%
dd-mmm-yyyya date05-Jan-2026
dddda dateMonday

To split at a character whose position varies, combine FIND with LEFT or MID: the first name in Asha Rao is =LEFT(A2,FIND(" ",A2)-1): take everything before the space (position minus one).

Tip

TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:A6) joins a whole range with a separator and skips blanks, which is handy for building a list in one cell.

Common mistakes

  • Doing maths on text that looks like a number: wrap it in VALUE first.
  • Forgetting the minus one in LEFT(A2,FIND(" ",A2)-1), which includes the space.
  • Hard-coding positions when the pieces vary in length: use FIND to locate the separator.

Check what you just learned

1. =MID("IN-2026-0042",4,4) returns:
  • IN
  • -2026
  • 0042
  • 2026 (correct)

Start at character 4 and take 4 characters.

2. Which function turns the text "42" into the number 42?
  • VALUE (correct)
  • TEXT
  • TRIM
  • FIND

VALUE converts text to a number.
keyPoints: LEFT, MID and RIGHT cut text; FIND locates a character.
VALUE turns text into a number; TEXT turns a number into formatted text.
& joins pieces of text.

topics.title: Dates are numbers
topics.html:
Excel stores a date as a serial number: the count of days since a starting day. 1 January 2026 is stored as 46023. That is why you can add days to a date and why subtracting two dates gives the number of days between them. The cell only shows it as a date because of its format.

The date toolkit
FunctionDoesExampleResult
DATE(y,m,d)Builds a date=DATE(2026,3,12)12-Mar-2026 (46093)
YEAR / MONTH / DAYPulls out a part=MONTH(B2)3
EDATE(date, n)Same day n months later=EDATE(B2,1)one month on
EOMONTH(date, n)Last day of the month n months on=EOMONTH(B2,0)31-Mar-2026
WEEKDAY(date, 2)Day of week, Monday = 1=WEEKDAY(B2,2)1 for Monday
NETWORKDAYS(a,b)Working days between two dates=NETWORKDAYS(B2,D2)9
DATEDIF(a,b,"Y")Whole years, months or days between=DATEDIF(A2,B2,"Y")age in years
Worked example

A project schedule

A task starts on 2 March 2026 and takes 10 days.

  1. Due date: =B2+C2 gives 12 March 2026 once the cell is formatted as a date.
  2. Working days: =NETWORKDAYS(B2,D2) counts Monday to Friday and includes both ends: 9.
  3. Month end: =EOMONTH(B2,0) gives 31 March 2026, handy for monthly reports.

Answer. Dates behave like numbers, so a schedule is just arithmetic.

Formula · Age in whole years

=DATEDIF(date_of_birth, today, "Y")

DATEDIF counts complete years. It is one of the few functions Excel does not list in the function picker, but it works.

Watch out

A date typed as text (for example 12.03.26) is not a date and will not calculate. If subtraction returns #VALUE!, check whether Excel really recognised the date; a date lines up on the right of the cell, text on the left.

Tip

Enter dates in an unambiguous form such as 2026-03-12 or build them with DATE. A date like 03/04/2026 means different things in different countries.

Try it yourself: How many days are there between 1 January and 31 January 2026?

Model answer. 30. Subtract the earlier date from the later one: the result counts the days between them (add 1 if you want to include both ends).

Check what you just learned

1. What does =B2+10 do when B2 holds a date?
  • Adds 10 months
  • Moves the date 10 days later (correct)
  • Shows an error
  • Adds 10 years

Dates are day counts, so adding 10 moves 10 days on.

2. Which function counts working days between two dates?
  • DATEDIF
  • EOMONTH
  • NETWORKDAYS (correct)
  • WEEKDAY

NETWORKDAYS counts Monday to Friday.
keyPoints: A date is a serial number shown with a date format.
Add days with +, subtract dates to count days.
EOMONTH and NETWORKDAYS handle month ends and working days.

topics.title: Data hygiene: consistent, unique, trustworthy
topics.html:
Clean formulas are no use on untidy data. Before analysing, check the data against a short list. Each check is a question you can answer with a formula.

A data hygiene checklist
CheckHow to test it
Numbers stored as text=COUNT(B2:B100) against =COUNTA(B2:B100): if the counts differ, some values are text
Duplicates=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$100,A2)>1 flags a repeated key
Blanks in required columns=COUNTBLANK(B2:B100)
Inconsistent spellingsA pivot or a sorted list reveals Kolkata and Calcutta side by side
Impossible valuesA negative quantity, a date in the future: =COUNTIF(C2:C100,"<0")
Extra spaces=SUMPRODUCT(--(LEN(A2:A100)<>LEN(TRIM(A2:A100)))) counts cells with spare spaces
Worked example

Find the duplicates

Customer IDs are in A2:A100. Some were entered twice.

  1. In B2 write =COUNTIF($A$2:$A$100,A2).
  2. Copy down. Any value above 1 is a repeated ID.
  3. Filter column B for values above 1 and review each pair before deleting anything.

Answer. Check before you delete: two rows with the same ID may be two real people.

A short routine before you trust a dataset

  1. Keep a copy of the raw data and work on another sheet.
  2. Run the checklist above and note what you found.
  3. Fix problems with formulas in new columns, so the steps are visible.
  4. Re-check totals against the raw data after cleaning.
  5. Write one line saying what you changed.
Watch out

Never delete the raw data. If the cleaning rule turns out to be wrong you will want to start again from the original.

Check what you just learned

1. COUNT is 90 and COUNTA is 100 for the same column. What does that suggest?
  • A chart is missing
  • The sheet is protected
  • Ten rows are duplicates
  • Ten values are text or non-numbers (correct)

COUNT counts only numbers, COUNTA counts everything that is not empty.

2. Before deleting an apparent duplicate you should:
  • Check whether it is really the same record (correct)
  • Delete it at once
  • Hide the column
  • Sort descending

Two rows with the same ID may still be different records.

Key terms: flip and sort

TRIM
Removes extra spaces
VALUE
Turns text into a number
Serial number
How Excel stores a date: a day count
EOMONTH
The last day of a month
NETWORKDAYS
Working days between two dates
Duplicate
A record that appears more than once
keyPoints: Test data for text numbers, duplicates, blanks and impossible values.
Clean in new columns and keep the raw data.
Re-check totals after cleaning.

modules.title: Analysis tools: summaries, charts and trends
modules.summary: Summarise data the way a PivotTable does, choose charts that answer questions, spot trends with statistics, and use what-if thinking.
modules.outcome: You can turn a long table into a summary, a chart and a forecast, and explain what the numbers do and do not show.
modules.intro: Analysis is the step between having data and knowing something. In this module you learn the tools analysts reach for first: summaries by group, a chart for every question, and simple statistics to measure a trend. You build the summary with formulas so that you see exactly what a PivotTable does.

topics.title: Tidy tables, sorting and filtering
topics.html:
Every analysis tool, including PivotTables, charts and the IFS functions, assumes your data is a tidy table: one heading row, one record per row, one fact per column, and nothing else in the way.

A tidy table
RegionProductUnitsRevenue
NorthPen10100
SouthPen20200
NorthBook5250

The rules of a tidy table

  • One row of headings, each heading unique and meaningful.
  • One record per row: do not put a subtotal row in the middle.
  • One kind of value per column: do not mix numbers and notes.
  • No blank rows or columns inside the data.
  • No merged cells: they break sorting, filtering and pivots.
Worked example

Sort and filter safely

You want the top-selling products.

  1. Select the whole table, not one column. Sorting one column alone scrambles the rows.
  2. Sort by Revenue, largest first.
  3. Filter Region to North to see one region, then clear the filter.
  4. Filters hide rows; they never delete them, so totals built with SUM still include hidden rows. Use SUBTOTAL when you want visible rows only.

Answer. A sorted, filtered view is an answer; the raw data stays intact.

Watch out

Sort the whole block, including the columns to the right. If formulas point at other rows, sorting can change what they refer to: sort the raw data first, then build formulas.

Tip

Turn the data into an Excel Table (Insert > Table). Formulas that point at a table grow automatically when you add rows.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are merged cells a problem for analysis?
  • They are slow
  • They break sorting, filtering and pivots (correct)
  • They are too wide
  • They hide formulas

Tools expect one value per cell.

2. What is wrong with sorting only one column of a table?
  • Nothing
  • It deletes headings
  • The rows no longer match across columns (correct)
  • It changes the font

The other columns stay where they were.
keyPoints: Tidy data: one heading row, one record per row, no blanks, no merged cells.
Always sort the whole table, never a single column.
Filters hide rows without deleting them.

topics.title: Summaries by group: what a PivotTable does
topics.html:
A PivotTable summarises a table by groups: regions down the side, products across the top, and the total of revenue in each cell. You drag fields into rows, columns and values; Excel does the sums. Underneath, every cell of a pivot is a SUMIFS.

Worked example

The same summary with one formula

Orders are in A1:C9 (Region, Product, Revenue). Regions are listed in F2:F5 and products in G1:H1.

  1. In G2 write =SUMIFS($C$2:$C$9,$A$2:$A$9,$F2,$B$2:$B$9,G$1).
  2. The data ranges are locked with $...$; the region is locked to column F with $F2; the product is locked to row 1 with G$1.
  3. Copy the formula across and down the grid. Each cell finds its own region and product.
  4. Add a row total with =SUM(G2:H2).

Answer. A grid of SUMIFS is a PivotTable you built yourself.

Pivot or formulas?
Use a PivotTable whenUse formulas when
You want to explore: regroup and re-slice quicklyThe report layout is fixed and shared with others
The data changes shape oftenYou need the summary inside a bigger model
You only need totals and countsYou need ratios, ranks and decisions beside the totals
Watch out

A PivotTable does not update on its own: after the data changes you must refresh it. A formula summary updates by itself. In the Yugty practice sheet you build the formula version, so the lab can check it; the reasoning is the same as for a pivot in desktop Excel.

Tip

Always add a total check: the grand total of your summary must equal the total of the raw data. If it does not, a category was missed or misspelled.

Check what you just learned

1. What is each cell of a PivotTable, in effect?
  • A VLOOKUP
  • A text value
  • A chart
  • A SUMIFS over the raw data (correct)

A pivot adds the values for one row group and one column group.

2. Why add a total check to a summary?
  • To catch categories that were missed or misspelled (correct)
  • To make it longer
  • To format it
  • To sort it

If the summary total differs from the data total, something was lost.
keyPoints: A PivotTable is a grid of group totals; each cell is a SUMIFS.
Mixed references let one SUMIFS fill a whole grid.
Check the grand total against the raw data.

topics.title: Charts that answer questions
topics.html:
A good chart answers one question in a few seconds. Choose the chart from the question, then remove everything that does not help.

Question to chart
The questionChartWhy
Which is biggest? How do categories compare?Bar or columnLength is the easiest thing to compare
How did it change over time?LineThe eye follows a trend
What share does each part take?Pie (few parts) or a stacked barParts of a whole
Are two measures related?ScatterShows the pattern between two numbers

Make the chart clear

  • A title that states the finding, not just the topic: North led every month beats Sales by region.
  • Sort the bars from largest to smallest unless there is a natural order.
  • Start bar charts at zero; a cut axis exaggerates differences.
  • Use one colour, and a second colour only for the bar you want noticed.
  • Label the units (rupees, thousands) once.

Common mistakes

  • Pie charts with many slices.
  • 3D effects that distort lengths.
  • A chart with no title or with Chart 1 as the title.
  • Charting the Total row together with the data, which dwarfs every other bar.
Tip

After you build the chart, cover the title and ask a colleague what it shows. If they cannot say in five seconds, simplify it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart best shows change over twelve months?
  • Pie
  • Line (correct)
  • Table
  • Radar

A line follows values through time.

2. Why start a bar chart at zero?
  • It looks tidier
  • Excel requires it
  • A cut axis exaggerates differences (correct)
  • To save space

Bar length should be proportional to the value.
keyPoints: Choose the chart from the question.
A title should state the finding.
Start bar charts at zero, and keep colours few.

topics.title: Statistics and forecasting
topics.html:
Three ideas turn a table into insight: the centre of the data, how spread out it is, and whether two measures are related.

The statistics toolkit
QuestionFunctionMeaning
What is typical?AVERAGE, MEDIANMEDIAN is not pulled around by extreme values
How spread out?STDEVA small value means points are close to the average
Are two things related?CORRELNear +1: rise together. Near 0: no relationship. Near -1: one rises as the other falls
What straight line fits?SLOPE, INTERCEPTHow much y changes per unit of x, and where the line starts
Worked example

Forecast the next month

Sales for six months are 102, 110, 121, 129, 141 and 150 (months 1 to 6, month in A2:A7 and sales in B2:B7).

  1. Slope: =SLOPE(B2:B7,A2:A7) is about 9.74: sales rise by about 9.7 a month.
  2. Intercept: =INTERCEPT(B2:B7,A2:A7) is 91.4.
  3. Month 7 forecast: =E3+E2*7 is about 159.6.
  4. Correlation: =CORREL(A2:A7,B2:B7) is about 0.999: the points sit almost exactly on a line, so a straight-line forecast is sensible.

Answer. Always check the correlation before trusting a straight-line forecast.

Forecast with a line

Choose the month to forecast and see the straight-line estimate.

Adjust Month to forecast and see Forecast sales, Rise per month change.

Watch out

Correlation is not causation. Two measures can move together because of a third reason, or by chance. A forecast is a reasonable guess, not a promise: the further ahead you look, the less you should trust it.

Common mistakes

  • Giving SLOPE the ranges the wrong way round: the y values (what you predict) come first.
  • Forecasting far beyond the data you have.
  • Reading a high correlation as proof that one thing causes the other.

Check what you just learned

1. A CORREL of 0.99 means:
  • No relationship
  • Both are constant
  • One causes the other
  • The two measures rise together very closely (correct)

Near +1 means they move together, which says nothing about causes.

2. In SLOPE(B2:B7,A2:A7), B holds:
  • The y values you want to predict (correct)
  • The x values
  • Dates
  • Weights

SLOPE takes y first, then x.

Key terms: flip and sort

Tidy table
One heading row, one record per row, no blanks
PivotTable
A summary of a table by groups
Correlation
How closely two measures move together
Slope
How much y changes per unit of x
Median
The middle value
Standard deviation
A measure of spread
keyPoints: MEDIAN resists extreme values; STDEV measures spread.
CORREL measures how closely two measures move together.
SLOPE and INTERCEPT give a straight-line forecast: check the correlation first.

modules.title: Finance and models
modules.summary: Price loans, compare investments with NPV and IRR, build a what-if model, and finish a workbook you would be comfortable sharing.
modules.outcome: You can answer 'what will it cost?' and 'is it worth it?' with a transparent, checked model that others can follow and change.
modules.intro: Spreadsheets earn their keep when money is involved: loan repayments, project returns, break-even points. Finance functions look intimidating, but each one answers a plain question. This module teaches the questions first, then the functions, and finishes with the habits that make a model trustworthy.

topics.title: Loans: PMT, PV, NPER and RATE
topics.html:
A loan has four numbers: the rate, the number of periods, the payment and the amount borrowed (the present value). Give Excel any three and it finds the fourth.

Loan functions
You know...You want...UseExample
Rate, periods, amountThe paymentPMT=PMT(0.01,12,60000)
Rate, periods, paymentThe amount you can borrowPV=PV(0.01,12,-5000)
Rate, payment, amountHow many periodsNPER=NPER(0.01,-6000,60000)
Periods, payment, amountThe rate per periodRATE=RATE(12,-5331,60000)
Worked example

A laptop loan

60,000 at 12% a year for 12 months.

  1. Monthly rate: 12% divided by 12 = 1% = 0.01. Rate and periods must use the same time unit.
  2. Payment: =PMT(0.01,12,60000) is about -5,330.93. The minus sign means money you pay out.
  3. Total paid: =-B5*B3 is about 63,971.13.
  4. Interest cost: total paid minus 60,000 is about 3,971.13.

Answer. Check your answer with a rough estimate: 12 payments of about 5,300 is about 63,600.

Price your own loan

Move the amount, the yearly rate and the months and watch the monthly payment and the interest cost.

Adjust Loan amount (rupees), Yearly rate (%), Months and see Monthly payment, Total interest change.

Watch out

Match the units. A yearly rate with monthly periods gives a wildly wrong payment. Divide the yearly rate by 12 when payments are monthly.

Common mistakes

  • Using the yearly rate with monthly periods.
  • Ignoring the sign: PMT returns a negative number for money you pay.
  • Forgetting fees: the rate in the formula is not the whole cost of a loan.

Check what you just learned

1. A loan has monthly payments. Which rate goes into PMT?
  • The yearly rate
  • The yearly rate divided by 12 (correct)
  • The yearly rate times 12
  • Any rate

The rate must match the payment period.

2. Which function finds how many months a payment would take?
  • PMT
  • PV
  • NPER (correct)
  • RATE

NPER returns the number of periods.
keyPoints: Rate, periods, payment and amount: give three, find the fourth.
Use the same time unit for the rate and the periods.
PMT is negative because it is money going out.

topics.title: Is it worth it? NPV and IRR
topics.html:
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year, because today's rupee can be invested or put to work. Net present value (NPV) translates future cash into today's money so projects can be compared fairly.

Two questions about an investment
QuestionToolDecision rule
How much better off am I, in today's money, at my required return?NPVPositive NPV: the project beats the required return
What return does the project itself earn?IRRCompare it with the return you require
Worked example

A new oven

An oven costs 100,000 now and brings extra cash of 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 over three years. The owner requires 10%.

  1. Discount the future cash: =NPV(B1,B3:B5) discounts years 1 to 3.
  2. Add the cost, which is today and so is not discounted: =NPV(B1,B3:B5)+B2 where B2 is -100,000.
  3. NPV is about 22,765: positive, so the oven beats the 10% requirement.
  4. =IRR(B2:B5) is about 21.6%: the oven earns more than the 10% needed.

Answer. Decision: invest. A negative NPV would mean skip, or ask for a better price.

What if the required return changes?

Move the discount rate and watch the NPV of the oven change.

Adjust Required return (%) and see NPV change.

Watch out

NPV in Excel discounts the first value by one full period. That is why the year 0 cash, which is not discounted, is added outside the NPV function.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the year 0 cost inside NPV, which discounts it as if it were a year away.
  • Comparing IRRs without looking at the size of the project.
  • Using one optimistic cash flow forecast: test a pessimistic one too.

Check what you just learned

1. A project has a positive NPV at your required return. This means:
  • It loses money
  • It costs nothing
  • Its IRR is zero
  • It beats the required return (correct)

A positive NPV means it earns more than you required.

2. Why is the year 0 cost added outside NPV?
  • Excel discounts every value inside NPV by at least one period (correct)
  • It is optional
  • It is secret
  • Excel cannot read negatives

NPV treats the first value as one period away.
keyPoints: NPV turns future cash into today's money.
Positive NPV beats the required return; IRR is the return the project earns.
Add the year 0 amount outside the NPV function.

topics.title: What-if models and break-even
topics.html:
A model is a sheet where you change an input and see what happens to the result. The art is keeping it simple, labelled and checkable.

Formula · Break-even units

break-even = fixed costs / (price - variable cost per unit)

Each unit sold contributes price minus variable cost towards the fixed costs. When contributions equal fixed costs, you break even.

Worked example

A stall at a fair

Fixed costs are 6,000. Each item sells for 120 and costs 70 to make.

  1. Contribution per item: 120 - 70 = 50.
  2. Break-even: 6,000 / 50 = 120 items.
  3. Profit at 200 items: 200 * 50 - 6,000 = 4,000.

Answer. Selling fewer than 120 means a loss; every item beyond adds 50 of profit.

A stall at a fair

Change the price, the cost and the items sold to see break-even and profit.

Adjust Price per item (rupees), Cost per item (rupees), Items sold and see Break-even items, Profit change.

The anatomy of a good model

  • Inputs in one labelled block, in a different colour.
  • Calculations that only point at inputs and other calculations.
  • Results at the top or on their own sheet.
  • Checks that must be zero or TRUE.
  • A short note saying what the model is for and who last changed it.
Watch out

A model is only as honest as its assumptions. Show the assumptions beside the result and test an unfavourable case before you share good news.

Tip

Use Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek in desktop Excel to work backwards: what price makes the profit 5,000? It changes one input until a result reaches the target.

Check what you just learned

1. Fixed costs are 6,000 and each item contributes 50. Break-even is:
  • 50 items
  • 120 items (correct)
  • 300 items
  • 6,050 items

6,000 divided by 50 is 120.

2. What belongs in an input block?
  • Results
  • Checks
  • Values you can change, labelled (correct)
  • Charts

Inputs are the numbers a user may change.
keyPoints: Break-even is fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit.
Separate inputs, calculations, results and checks.
State assumptions and test an unfavourable case.

topics.title: Finishing a workbook others can trust
topics.html:
A workbook is finished when a stranger can open it, understand it, change an input and trust the answer. These last steps take ten minutes and prevent most embarrassment.

The finishing checklist

  1. Test with easy numbers where you know the answer.
  2. Check totals two ways (for example column totals and row totals must agree).
  3. Scan for errors: look for error codes, text left-aligned in number columns and numbers that look too good.
  4. Label every input, every sheet and every unit.
  5. Format consistently: the same number format, no rainbow colours.
  6. Protect the formulas (Review > Protect Sheet) and leave only the inputs editable.
  7. Save a clear file name with a date or version, and keep an unprotected master.
  8. Explain the model in a short note: purpose, inputs, results, known limits.
Sharing choices
You want people to...Share as
Read onlyPDF, or a copy with values only (Paste Special > Values)
Change the inputsA protected workbook with unlocked input cells
Collaborate liveA shared online workbook, with a named owner
Reuse the modelA template with the inputs cleared and a note
Watch out

Before sharing a file outside your organisation, check for hidden sheets, comments and names you did not intend to share. Paste values into a fresh file if in doubt.

Worked example

A ten-minute review

You are about to send a sales model to a manager.

  1. Change a key input to a round number and check the result by hand.
  2. Make sure the check cells show zero.
  3. Protect the formulas and lock the sheet.
  4. Add a note saying what the model does and what it does not.

Answer. A reviewed, labelled, protected model builds trust faster than any clever formula.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test a model with easy numbers?
  • It is faster
  • To hide errors
  • Excel prefers them
  • You can see at once whether the answer is right (correct)

Easy numbers let you verify by hand.

2. How can you stop people overwriting formulas?
  • Protect the sheet with only inputs unlocked (correct)
  • Colour them red
  • Rename the file
  • Hide the ribbon

Sheet protection locks every cell except the ones you unlock.

Key terms: flip and sort

PMT
The payment on a loan
Present value
Future money expressed in today's terms
NPV
Net present value of a series of cash flows
IRR
The return a project itself earns
Break-even
Where income equals costs
Model
A sheet where changing an input updates the result
keyPoints: Test with easy numbers and check totals two ways.
Label inputs, units and sheets; protect formulas.
Choose the sharing format to match what people should do with it.

practical.intro: Model a real choice: a loan, a course fee or a small business idea.
steps: List the inputs (cost, rate, time, income) in a labelled block.

capstone.title: Final project: regional performance dashboard
capstone.summary: Build a complete dashboard and pass the final assessment.
capstone.intro: You now have the toolkit of an analyst: mixed references, logic, lookups, conditional totals, ranking, cleaning, summaries, charts and finance. In this final step you build a dashboard in the spreadsheet lab: actual revenue per region from raw data with SUMIFS, percent of target, a status, a rank, the best region by name, the company total and a chart. Then take the final assessment, which covers the whole course.
steps: Work through the Regional performance dashboard lab: SUMIFS on the raw data, percent of target, nested IF status, RANK, INDEX with MATCH, a total and a bar chart.
Test the dashboard: change one revenue figure and check that every result follows.
Look for errors and check the company total against the raw data by adding the twelve revenue figures.
Take the final assessment below.
